name: Code Verification Does Not Establish Economic Effects
text:
Code establishes a model's implementation. Economic effects require separate evidence. Gräbner's validation framework explains the distinction. Model verification tests whether a computational model does what its designer intended. Validation asks whether the model reasonably represents its target and assesses the model's relationship to reality. His framework also requires an explicit key between model properties and target-system properties. Validation becomes necessary when the model is used to make informed statements about the real world.

This independently qualifies Kaal's claim. Formal objects and source code can make a mechanism explicit and testable. They do not show that the named economic effect occurred. That inference requires observable target properties and an appropriate validation design.

The source concerns computational models generally. The analysis does not evaluate Kaal's framework, observables, code, or evidence. It supplies a methodological boundary. No economic effect follows from that boundary.

sourceProvenance.sourceProposition: Gräbner distinguishes verification of a computational model's internal implementation from validation of its relation to a target system and reality. His framework requires a key linking model properties to target-system properties, and it makes validation necessary before informed real-world statements are drawn from the model.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: The third step is to link the properties of the model, P , to the relevant properties of the target system, Q.
Model validation means to test whether the model is actually a reasonable representation of the target (Rand & Rust 2011, p. 187).
In contrast to verification, these four activities assess the relation of the model to reality.
Validation becomes necessary as soon as we want to use a model to make informed statements about the real world (e.g., Schulze et al. 2017).
